questions.q: In C, what marks the end of a string stored in a char array?
choices: The declared size of the array
A length value stored before the first character
questions.explain: C has no separate string type. A string is an array of char values ended by the null character '\0'.

questions.q: Every array of char values is a C string.
questions.explain: Every C string is an array of char, but a char array is only a C string if it ends with a '\0' character.

questions.q: Which printf placeholder prints the value of a C string?
questions.explain: Use %s to print a string. (%c prints a single char.)
strcpy copies "hi" (and its '\0') into str2. Changing str2[1] to 'o' gives "ho". str1 is unchanged, so the output is "hi ho".

questions.q: strlen(str) returns 5 for str = "Hello". How many chars must you malloc to hold a copy of str made with strcpy?
questions.explain: strlen does not count the terminating '\0', so you need strlen(str) + 1 = 6 chars: malloc(sizeof(char) * (size+1)).

questions.q: How many bytes does the string "hello world" occupy in memory, counting its terminating null character?
questions.explain: 11 visible characters (including the space) plus 1 for '\0' gives 12. That is why strcpy into a char mystr[5] overflows the array.

questions.q: Which of these code fragments have a memory error?
questions.explain: (1) writes 12 bytes into a 5-byte array. (2) writes through a NULL destination. (3) changes a read-only string literal. (4) is fine because 32 bytes is enough room.

questions.q: strcpy and strcat allocate enough memory for their result, so the destination pointer does not need to point to space that is already large enough.
questions.explain: These functions write through the destination pointer and assume it already has enough space. The caller must allocate it. If it doesn't, the behavior is undefined: anything from a crash to a security vulnerability.

questions.category: char[] vs char* and comparing strings
questions.q: Given char buf[32]; and a function char *get_name(void);, why is buf = get_name(); not allowed?
choices: A statically declared array name is not a valid lvalue, because its base address cannot change
get_name would have to return char[] instead of char *
buf would first have to be set to NULL
questions.explain: You can only assign a char * return value to a char * variable. A static array's name refers to a fixed base address and cannot be assigned to.

questions.category: char[] vs char* and comparing strings
questions.q: You can pass both a statically declared char array and a dynamically allocated char array to a function whose parameter is declared char *.
questions.explain: Either kind of array name evaluates to the array's base address, so both work for a char * (or char []) parameter.

questions.category: char[] vs char* and comparing strings
questions.q: d_str points to a heap char array and str is a stack char array. What does the expression (d_str == str) compare?
choices: The base addresses of the two arrays
The characters of the two strings, one at a time
The lengths of the two strings
Only the first character of each string
questions.explain: == compares addresses, not contents. Use strcmp or strncmp (or a hand-written loop) to compare the characters.

questions.category: char[] vs char* and comparing strings
questions.q: What does strcmp("aaa", "Zoo") return?
questions.explain: strcmp compares ASCII values. 'a' has a larger ASCII code than 'Z', so "aaa" counts as greater than "Zoo".

questions.category: char[] vs char* and comparing strings
questions.q: What does strcmp("aaa", "zoo") return?
questions.explain: 'a' has a smaller ASCII code than 'z', so "aaa" is less than "zoo" and the result is negative.

questions.category: char[] vs char* and comparing strings
questions.q: str holds "alligator". What does strncmp(str, "all", 3) return?
questions.explain: strncmp compares at most n characters. The first 3 characters match, so it returns 0.

questions.q: After strcpy(str, "Hello There");, what does strlen(str) return?
questions.explain: strlen counts the characters up to the '\0' but not the '\0' itself. That's 11 here, including the space.

questions.q: str holds "Hello There". After strncpy(d_str, str, 5); (and nothing else), what is in d_str?
choices: All of "Hello There", because strncpy stops only at '\0'
questions.explain: If src has size or more characters, strncpy copies exactly size characters and does not add a '\0'. You must add it yourself, e.g. d_str[5] = '\0';.
strlcpy copies at most size-1 characters and always adds '\0' (if size > 0). To get 5 characters plus the terminator, pass size 6.

questions.q: strcpy is safe to use even when the source string may be longer than the destination array, because it stops copying when the destination is full.
questions.explain: strcpy copies until it reaches the '\0' in src and has no idea how big dst is. When src might be too long, use strncpy (or strlcpy) instead.
strcat appends " stripes". Then strncat appends only the first 8 characters of " are black.", which are " are bla" (spaces count).
strstr returns a pointer to where "trip" starts inside str. Printing from that point to the '\0' gives "tripes are bla".
strchr returns a pointer to the first 'e' (index 1), so printing from there gives "ebra fish stripes are bla".

questions.q: What do strstr and strchr return when the substring or character is not found?
choices: A pointer to the string's '\0' character
questions.explain: Both return NULL when there is no match, so check for NULL before using the result.

questions.q: When strchr(s, c) finds c, what does it return?
choices: The address of the first matching char inside s
The integer index of the first match
A newly malloc'd copy of the rest of the string
The address of the last matching char inside s
questions.explain: It returns a pointer into the original array at the first occurrence. That position starts a '\0'-terminated run of chars, so it can be used as a string.

questions.q: In a loop that calls strtok repeatedly to get every token from line, what is the first argument on every call after the first one?
choices: The token returned by the previous call
questions.explain: The first call is strtok(line, delim). Each later call is strtok(NULL, delim), which continues in the same string.

questions.q: How does strtok tell you there are no more tokens?
choices: It returns 0 cast to an int
questions.explain: A loop like while (token != NULL) { ...; token = strtok(NULL, delim); } stops when strtok returns NULL.

questions.q:
The delimiter string is " \t\f\r\v\n" (whitespace). How many tokens does strtok find in this input line?

"        aaaaa             bbbbbbbbb          cccccc\n"
questions.explain: Tokens are separated by any number of delimiter characters, so the leading, repeated, and trailing whitespace is skipped. The tokens are aaaaa, bbbbbbbbb, and cccccc.

questions.q: How does sprintf differ from printf?
choices: It writes the formatted result into a char array instead of to the terminal
It reads formatted input from a string
It uses different placeholders from printf
It can only format strings, not numbers
questions.explain: sprintf(char *s, const char *format, ...) uses printf-style placeholders but stores the result in s.

answer: Henry is 12 years old and in grade 7
questions.explain: Each placeholder is filled with a char representation of the matching argument, in order.

questions.q: What is the value of atoi("1234") + 1?
questions.explain: atoi converts the string "1234" to the int 1234, and adding 1 gives 1235.

questions.q: What value does atof("4.56") return?
questions.explain: atof converts a string to a floating-point value (a double).

answer: i see XX zebras, goats, and cows
questions.explain: Uppercase letters become lowercase, and each digit in "20" becomes 'X'. The 'X' chars are written into str and not tested again, so they stay uppercase.

questions.q: Which library has functions for testing and changing individual char values, such as isdigit and toupper?
questions.explain: ctype.h contains the functions for individual characters. string.h is for whole C strings.

questions.q: What do test functions like isupper(ch) and isdigit(ch) return when the test is true?
questions.explain: They return a non-zero value for true and 0 for false. Check the result with if (isupper(ch)), not with == 1.

questions.q: Which of these calls return a non-zero (true) value?
questions.explain: 'Z' is an uppercase letter, so isupper and isalpha are true. '7' is a digit, so isalnum (letter or digit) is true. 'Z' is neither lowercase nor a digit.
